headline: Ukraine talks resume, Colom's lead grows, oil steadies near US$92
briefing: Russia and Ukraine are back at the table in Abu Dhabi for a second day, with a large prisoner swap under discussion but no deal on territory. In the U.S., Democrat Scott Colom's Mississippi Senate lead grew to about 3,000 votes as hotter-than-expected October inflation raised odds of another Federal Reserve hike. Oil is holding near US$92, and in Ontario the province's hand-picked regional chairs, including Steven Del Duca in York, face conflict-of-interest criticism.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.
stories.headline: Oil steadies near US$92 as markets weigh Iran deal hopes against Hormuz risks
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, which would ease fuel and delivery costs. A failed deal or new attacks on shipping could quickly reverse the drop.
stories.now: Brent rose about 0.6% to roughly US$92 a barrel early Wednesday and U.S. benchmark WTI was near US$86, after Brent briefly slipped below US$90 on Tuesday for the first time since August. The slide followed Monday's White House meeting with Qatar's prime minister, who reportedly carried an Iranian plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade and freeing about US$8 billion in Iranian funds held in Qatar; neither government has confirmed those terms. Trump said new strikes look unlikely and the war could end fairly soon, but Iran's security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei has dismissed talk of negotiations. Attacks on tankers near Hormuz continue, and several analysts doubt a durable deal is close.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.
stories.headline: Colom's Mississippi lead nears 3,000 as Hinds County ballots loom
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.
stories.now: Late Tuesday the AP had Democrat Scott Colom ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,990 votes with about 98% counted, after Tuesday's deadline for absentee ballots to arrive. Hinds County, a Democratic stronghold, is expected to upload its outstanding affidavit ballots on Wednesday, and counties must send official results to Secretary of State Michael Watson by Friday; Hyde-Smith's campaign says thousands of votes remain in Republican counties, and Mississippi has no recount law. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola had 118,926 first-choice votes (49%) to Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's 114,676 (47.2%) in Tuesday's update; with no one at 50%, the ranked-choice count runs on Nov. 18. The Justice Department has also sued to block certification of Alaska's results, a claim Peltola rejects.

stories.backstory: Ontario first gave 'strong mayor' powers to Toronto and Ottawa in 2022 and later extended them to dozens of cities. This spring the province brought in the Better Regional Governance Act, letting it appoint chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka, Peel, Waterloo and York and the Simcoe warden, and cutting the size of Niagara's council. Some of these posts were previously chosen by voters or by regional councillors. The appointments come right after the Oct. 26 municipal elections.
stories.headline: Markham mayor calls Del Duca's York appointment a conflict of interest
stories.impact: For York, Peel, Durham and Halton residents, regional chairs now have more say over budgets that drive property taxes and over approvals for housing and infrastructure. Watch the first regional budgets under the new chairs.
stories.now: Municipal Affairs Minister Rob Flack named Kevin Ashe (Durham), Ann Mulvale (Halton), Scott Aitchison (Muskoka), Frank Campion (Niagara), Nando Iannicca (Peel), Scott Davey (Waterloo), Steven Del Duca (York) and Don McIsaac as Simcoe County warden. Del Duca, a former Ontario Liberal leader, will chair York Region while staying on as mayor of Vaughan, and Markham Mayor Frank Scarpitti called that arrangement a blatant conflict of interest. Ford praised Del Duca as one of the best mayors in the province, while NDP critic Jeff Burch said the appointments undermine local democracy. The chairs can hire or fire the chief administrative officer (the top civil servant) and department heads, veto some bylaws and propose the regional budget; the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) said it looks forward to working with them.

stories.backstory: The bank cut its key rate to 2.25% in October 2025 as tariffs slowed the economy. Energy prices then surged with the Iran war, and annual inflation reached 3.1% in September, although core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the bank raised its rate a quarter point to 2.5%, its first hike in about three years, and said further increases might be needed.
stories.headline: Bank of Canada notes show oil shock drove its October rate hike
stories.impact: GTA homeowners with variable-rate mortgages or renewing soon should watch Dec. 9. If oil keeps falling, pressure for another increase may ease; if it rebounds, borrowing costs could rise again.
stories.now: The Bank of Canada published its summary of Governing Council talks on Tuesday afternoon. Members considered two options, holding the policy rate at 2.25% or raising it to 2.5%, and the main reason they hiked was that oil prices tied to the Middle East war were expected to stay elevated. They also judged that stronger growth would use up spare capacity in the economy and that rising business costs would eventually show up in core inflation. Since the decision, Brent crude has fallen about 25% from its late-October peak, which could ease that worry. The next rate decision is Dec. 9.

stories.summary: The central bank's summary of its Oct. 28 deliberations says officials weighed holding at 2.25% against hiking to 2.5%, and chose the hike mainly because oil prices looked set to stay high for longer.
stories.why: The bank's rate sets the prime rate that variable mortgages and lines of credit follow. Its reasoning shows that falling oil prices could reduce the case for another hike.

stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.
stories.headline: Russia-Ukraine talks enter second day as sides discuss big prisoner swap
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would feel the effects of any change in security arrangements.
stories.now: Russian and Ukrainian delegations, with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, returned to the table in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday after nearly four hours of talks on Tuesday, the first trilateral round in about nine months. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the first day constructive and said humanitarian issues such as prisoner exchanges and the return of children were discussed; he reportedly said the sides are considering swapping 1,000 or possibly 1,500 prisoners each. Russia's delegation is led by Vladimir Medinsky. Big gaps remain over territory, security guarantees and ceasefire terms, which Zelenskyy says will ultimately need to be settled by leaders. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks productive but urged patience and said Europe should eventually join the format.

stories.headline: U.S. prices rise 0.4% in October as energy costs bite
stories.summary: The U.S. consumer price index rose 0.4% in October, above forecasts, keeping pressure on the Federal Reserve ahead of its December decision.
stories.now: The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said consumer prices rose 0.4% in October after a 0.6% jump in September, beating the 0.3% economists expected. Energy rose 0.7%, food 0.5% and shelter 0.3%, while core prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3% for a third straight month. The BLS did not publish a year-over-year rate because last year's government shutdown stopped October 2025 data collection; one economist puts the implied annual pace around 4%. Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi said the report makes a December rate increase more likely.
stories.backstory: Oil prices surged after the U.S.-Iran war began in February and the Strait of Hormuz was choked, pushing up fuel and shipping costs. U.S. inflation has run well above the Fed's 2% target for months, and tariffs have added to the price of many imported goods. The Fed and the Bank of Canada both announce rate decisions on Dec. 9.
stories.why: Hotter U.S. inflation makes another Fed hike more likely, which tends to push up borrowing costs and the U.S. dollar.
stories.impact: A stronger U.S. dollar makes cross-border shopping and U.S. travel pricier for GTA residents. Rate moves in the U.S. also influence Canadian fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada's December thinking.

stories.backstory: Massie's articles centre on the Iran war, which he says has run more than 90 days without approval from Congress, and also cite operations in Venezuela and Yemen. He first filed them in the fall, but the House left early for the campaign. Democrats won the House in the Nov. 3 midterms and take control in January; their leader Hakeem Jeffries calls himself a hard yes on impeachment.
stories.headline: House shelves Hegseth impeachment in 211-204 vote
stories.impact: The effects for Ontario are indirect: fights over the Iran war and Pentagon policy can shape oil prices and U.S. defence and trade priorities. Watch for how a divided Washington handles tariffs and Canada talks.
stories.now: The motion to refer the eight articles to committee passed 211-204, with Massie the only Republican voting with all Democrats against it. Referral means there will be no floor vote on impeachment before the current Congress ends in January. Hegseth called the push a farce and a political spectacle, and the Pentagon hailed the result. Massie, who is retiring after losing his primary, has said he will not file another resolution. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the vote is just the beginning, and Democrats take control of the House in January.

stories.backstory: Canada has used remission and relief measures to soften the cost of counter-tariffs on its own importers. A recent Finance Canada report found Ottawa approved about $5.6 billion in relief against a projected $2.2 billion, with more than 800 requests still unresolved.
stories.headline: Ottawa widens tariff relief as Carney says Trump still calls the shots on trade
stories.impact: Schools and some public bodies in Ontario may face lower costs on imported goods. Businesses importing affected goods may be able to apply for relief.
stories.now: The federal government extended its tariff relief program beyond U.S. steel imports, so goods used by public education bodies, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations, can also qualify; Newsweek reports the program now runs to June 30, 2028, while exemptions are being withdrawn for some U.S. goods where Canadian alternatives exist. On Tuesday, Carney said the Trump administration remains the main authority on trade agreements even after Democrats won Congress, and Ottawa will keep working toward a deal that suits Canada. Democrats have pledged to try to repeal tariffs on Canada, but they would need Republican votes to override a veto. Trump has also threatened new tariffs on Canadian vehicles starting in January.

stories.backstory: A federal public inquiry found that China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canada's democratic institutions. Relations soured for years over arrests, tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and Chinese duties on Canadian canola. Carney's government has since sought to rebuild trade ties with Beijing as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports, which drew a tariff threat from Trump over any Canada-China deal.
stories.headline: Carney to press Xi on foreign interference at APEC in Shenzhen
stories.impact: GTA residents with family or business ties to China are among those most exposed to interference concerns. Any trade easing could matter for Ontario exporters and for car buyers, while friction with the U.S. over China ties could complicate Canada-U.S. trade talks.
stories.now: Carney said Tuesday he will use the meeting on the APEC sidelines to stress that Canada expects non-interference from China and other countries. He also plans to discuss global security and what he called a deepening economic partnership with clear guardrails. It will be his second in-person meeting with Xi this year, after a visit to China in January. Opposition critics and China watchers have questioned the shift in tone from the 2025 election campaign, when Carney named China as Canada's top geopolitical threat. Beijing has long denied interfering in Canadian politics.

stories.backstory: Ontario's EBR, passed in 1993, lets residents comment on proposed environmental decisions and, in some cases, seek leave to appeal permits. The Ford government has repeatedly moved to fast-track projects, including 2025's Bill 5, which weakened species-at-risk protections and allowed special economic zones. It also exempted the proposed Dresden landfill from a full environmental assessment, a move local councils still oppose.
stories.headline: Experts warn Ford's Bill 140 would gut Ontario's Environmental Bill of Rights
stories.impact: GTA residents near proposed developments, aggregate pits or waste sites may have fewer ways to object or appeal. You can still comment on the Environmental Registry of Ontario until Nov. 26.
stories.now: Bill 140, the Building Ontario Faster Act, 2026, was tabled on Oct. 27 and would amend 23 laws and create two new ones. Critics focus on Schedule 8, which rewrites the Environmental Bill of Rights (EBR); Richard Lindgren of the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA) says the law would keep its name but lose the legal rights people actually use. Groups including Environmental Defence say it would weaken public consultation, remove appeal rights and drop some notices from the Environmental Registry of Ontario. The bill also changes the Environmental Assessment Act and the Environmental Protection Act. The province has said the changes are meant to speed up housing and infrastructure.

stories.backstory: Champagne announced the Nov. 5 date on Oct. 20. The budget arrives while U.S. tariffs remain in place and the Bank of Canada has just raised its rate to 2.50%, its first hike since 2023.
stories.headline: Carney government's second budget projects $62.3B deficit with $142B in new spending
stories.impact: Watch for small-business tax changes, the deficit figure and immigration targets, which affect GTA hiring, rents and housing demand.
stories.now: The budget projects a $62.3-billion deficit for 2026-27, reported as down from $65.3 billion in the spring forecast, with deficits above $50 billion in each of the next four years. It adds roughly $142.1 billion in new spending over five years, much of it classed as capital spending. Debt interest is projected to reach about $85.5 billion a year by the end of the decade. Commentators are split between those who call it fiscally measured for bond markets and those who say it borrows too much. The Liberals still need opposition support in the House of Commons to pass it. The immigration levels update was expected alongside it; details were not confirmed in this run. Coverage also highlights a plan to end homelessness in Canada within ten years, focused on transitional housing and work with the provinces, and spending meant to strengthen economic and cultural sovereignty, paid for in part by an oil-revenue windfall.

stories.backstory: In 2023 Toronto faced a large budget hole. Ford and Chow agreed a package that included the province taking over the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway, with roughly $1.2 billion over three years. That deal is now winding down, and the city has been seeking more help.
stories.headline: Toronto freezes most hiring as it faces a $1.1-billion budget gap
stories.impact: Toronto residents could face higher property taxes, TTC fares or service pressure in the next city budget if no new money arrives.
stories.now: Mayor Olivia Chow confirmed on Nov. 6 that the city has frozen most hiring, exempting essential roles such as paramedics and firefighters; recruitments without an offer already made are halted, and no end date has been set. City documents suggest the 2027 gap could grow by nearly $500 million, and the TTC estimates the end of provincial funding leaves it about $379 million short next year. Ford said on Nov. 4 that the province is in tough times and will not sign a new funding deal; Chow says she will keep negotiating piece by piece. The city is also doing a line-by-line review of spending.

stories.headline: U.S. charges three men in alleged Iran-backed plots, including UK air base attack
stories.summary: Federal prosecutors in New York charged three men accused of helping direct nearly 20 attacks or attempts in Europe and the U.S. and planning an assault on RAF Fairford in England.
stories.now: An indictment unsealed Tuesday names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, 32, Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, 35. Prosecutors say they acted for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah, targeting Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. and plotting in September against RAF Fairford, a British base used by U.S. B-1 bombers in the Iran war. Al-Saadi, described as a Kata'ib Hezbollah commander, was already jailed in New York and is accused of passing coded messages from prison. Attorney General Todd Blanche said anyone plotting against bases housing U.S. troops will be prosecuted.
stories.backstory: Since the U.S. and Israel began striking Iran in February, Western officials have warned of Iran-linked plots abroad. Britain has made several arrests under its National Security Act tied to Iranian intelligence. RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire has hosted U.S. bombers flying missions against Iran.
stories.why: The case shows the Iran war spilling into security threats far from the Middle East, including against Western bases and Jewish communities.
stories.impact: There is no known Canadian link, but Canadian security agencies watch such networks closely. Expect continued heightened security at Jewish community sites and some military facilities.

stories.headline: Remembrance Day: road closures downtown and a TTC pause at 11 a.m.
stories.summary: Ceremonies across the GTA mark Remembrance Day, with downtown Toronto road closures and a two-minute TTC service pause at 11 a.m.
stories.now: Toronto holds its ceremony at the Old City Hall Cenotaph, 60 Queen St. W., at 10:45 a.m., and Queen's Park holds one at the same time; police expect road closures from around 10 a.m. and advise drivers to allow extra time. The TTC will pause all service for two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. In Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected to lay a wreath at the National War Memorial, where three Second World War veterans and about 300 cadets are expected. This year marks 25 years since Canada's mission in Afghanistan began.
stories.backstory: Remembrance Day marks the 1918 armistice that ended the First World War and honours Canadians who served and died in conflicts since. It is not a statutory holiday in Ontario, so most businesses and schools stay open, while federal workers get the day off. This year's ceremonies follow the Oct. 17 fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta that killed four soldiers and injured 39; three investigations are under way.

timeline.event: Fire at CFB Wainwright kills four soldiers

stories.why: It is the country's main day to honour military service, and this year comes weeks after a deadly training accident.
stories.impact: Expect downtown Toronto road closures near Queen and Bay and around Queen's Park late morning, and a brief TTC stop at 11 a.m. Most Ontario stores and services are open; federal offices and Canada Post are closed.
